name: Shabu-shabu (beef swished in broth)
text: Thin-sliced beef swished through hot broth at the table. The usual account traces it to Chinese huoguo (itself said to come from Mongolia), brought to Japan by folk-craft leader Yoshida Shoya, who ate it in China as a wartime army doctor, and introduced as 'beef mizutaki' around 1945. The name was coined in 1952 by Miyake Chuichi at Suehiro in Eiraku-cho, Osaka, after the sight and sound of rinsing oshibori in a basin.
flavor: Light and brothy; the beef is cooked only by passing it through the pot (kuguraseru).
use: Served as a table-cooked nabe: raw sliced beef and vegetables cooked by the diner in a shared pot of dashi, then dipped.
craft: Provenance is disputed, so quote it with care: sources split between Kyoto's Junidanya and Osaka's Suehiro as the origin venue, and Wikipedia says Yoshida called it 'beef susugi-nabe' (rinsing pot). One source argues the name is not an onomatopoeia for meat swimming. The results seen give no broth, slice-thickness or timing specifications.
src: Oggi: why is it called shabu-shabu

name: Anko-nabe and dobujiru (Ibaraki monkfish hotpot)
text: Ibaraki's winter monkfish nabe. Restaurants and inns in the prefecture commonly serve it from about November to March. One regional-cuisine listing describes the Ibaraki style as a 'dobujiru' pot in which the liver (kimo) is dissolved into the broth.
flavor: Rich, liver-thickened broth in the dobujiru style.
use: Served as a seasonal hotpot at inns and restaurants around Oarai and Mito, in winter.
craft: The point of the dobujiru style is dissolving the liver into the pot. The sources seen do not give liver ratio, seasoning or cutting method, so check those with the local maker rather than assuming them.

name: Kaki no dote-nabe (Hiroshima oyster pot)
text: A Hiroshima local dish in which miso is smeared around the inside rim of the pot and oysters, tofu and vegetables are simmered while the miso is gradually melted in. The leading explanation of the name is that the miso wall looks like a dote (embankment); other accounts say it was devised by itinerant peddlers.
flavor: Miso-forward, with the broth gradually becoming richer as the rim melts.
use: Cooked at the table in an earthen or iron pot in the oyster season; diners control how much miso to bring into the broth.
craft: The distinguishing technique is the miso 'bank' on the rim, not a pre-mixed miso broth. Origin is uncertain (embankment theory versus peddler theory), so do not state one as fact.

name: Tessa and tecchiri (Osaka fugu sashimi and fugu nabe)
text: Osaka's names for fugu sashimi and fugu chirinabe. Tessa is explained as 'teppo no sashimi' and tecchiri as 'teppo no chirinabe', teppo being fugu slang. Fugu eating goes back to the Jomon period; a ban followed poisoning deaths in Hideyoshi's time, and in the Meiji era selling raw fugu was prohibited nationwide. One researcher notes that in Osaka the law was ignored and a tecchiri boom occurred in the early Showa years.
flavor: Clean white flesh, eaten raw as sashimi or simmered in a chiri pot.
use: Core courses of fugu kaiseki in Osaka and Shimonoseki, usually sashimi first and the pot after.
craft: Fugu handling is licensed work; Shimonoseki is said to have the most certified fugu detoxification craftsmen in Japan. The results seen do not give slice thickness, plating or pot-broth details, and the Osaka-boom claim comes from a single social-media post, so treat it as a lead.
src: Mainichi Grill-bu: history of fugu cuisine
Yamatoya Honten: fugu ban and Osaka

name: Fuku of Shimonoseki (fugu ban and its lifting)
text: Shimonoseki calls fugu 'fuku' and bills itself as the place where fugu eating was lifted from prohibition. The popular story has Ito Hirobumi, lodging at the Shunpanro, being served forbidden fugu by the proprietress, then urging the prefectural governor to lift the ban. Sources give the year as 1887 (Meiji 20) or 1888 (Meiji 21), and one researcher calls the whole tale a widespread fabrication.
flavor: Not applicable; this is a cultural and regulatory history entry.
use: Context for menus and storytelling at Shimonoseki fugu restaurants.
craft: Be careful with the Ito Hirobumi anecdote: the date differs by source and it is contested. The name 'fuku' is explained as a local preference, while 'fugu' spread via Tokyo after the ban was lifted. A merchant's diary from the late Edo period reportedly records fugu as a drinking snack in Shimonoseki.

Hidaka Honten: why Shimonoseki says fuku

name: Katsudon: the Kofu, Waseda and Osaka claims
text: Pork cutlet over rice, with several competing origin stories. The Kofu claim holds that the soba shop Okumura Honten was serving katsudon in the late Meiji 30s (roughly the 1900s), based on a September 1995 article in the Yamanashi Nichinichi Shimbun. Rival claims point to Waseda (1921-22) and Osaka (1921). The Kofu claim is described as the most prominent of the three.
flavor: Cutlet, rice and sauce; the Kofu claim is described as 'cutlet rice put straight into a bowl'.
use: Teishoku and soba-shop staple; the regional style (egg-bound or sauced) is part of how it is judged.
craft: When quoting an origin, name the claim and its basis. The Kofu claim rests on a 1995 local newspaper article, not a primary document. The results seen do not detail the egg-bound versus sauce styles, so verify those locally.
src: Nikkei: Is Kofu the birthplace of katsudon?

name: Oyakodon: Tokyo and Osaka origin claims
text: Chicken and egg over rice. Tokyo and Osaka each claim it: Tokyo's Tamahide in Nihonbashi Ningyocho (dated about 1887 in one source, about 1893 in another) and Osaka's Torikiku (said to have been devised for the 1903 Fifth National Industrial Exposition). The earliest documented use found is an 1884 newspaper advertisement for Edokou in Motomachi, Kobe.
flavor: Soft egg and chicken over rice.
use: Classic bowl at chicken specialists and soba or udon shops.
craft: Dates conflict across sources, so cite the documentary evidence (the 1884 Kobe advertisement) separately from the shop legends. The results seen give no information on egg-set timing or dashi ratios.
src: Chikuma Shobo: Iino Ryoichi on the five great donburi

name: Tendon: origin of the tempura bowl
text: Tempura over rice. It is said to have appeared after unadon. An older account credits Hashizen, a soba yatai in Shinbashi, in 1831; another source gives Tenpo 8, and mentions that Tenpo 2 is also cited, so the dating varies by a few years.
flavor: Tempura glazed with sauce over rice.
use: Edo-style soba and tempura shops serve it as a quick bowl.
craft: The results seen cover only origin dates, not the Edo versus Kyoto sauce and batter differences. Do not assume those distinctions without a specific source; cite the date as uncertain (1831 versus Tenpo 8).

name: Unadon (eel on rice)
text: Described as the first donburi to appear, arising in the Edo period, with tendon following it. Food historian Iino Ryoichi treats it as one of five great donburi (tendon, katsudon, gyudon, unadon, oyakodon) in a Chikuma Gakugei Bunko book on their birth.
flavor: Grilled eel with sauce over rice.
use: Eaten year-round, with a peak around the Doyo no ushi day.
craft: The results seen give no details of grilling or tare. Use it as the historical anchor for the other donburi: unadon first, tendon second.

name: Doyo no ushi no hi eel custom
text: The custom of eating eel on the ox day of the summer doyo. The popular story credits Hiraga Gennai, who had an eel shop put up a sign saying 'today is the ox day'. Whether Gennai really did this is uncertain, and the late-Edo book Toto Saijiki already records the custom as established. An older custom of eating foods starting with 'u' (udon, umeboshi) is also cited.
flavor: Not applicable; this is a seasonal custom.
use: Peak demand day for unagi shops in July.
craft: Treat the Gennai story as a marketing legend, not a documented fact. The calendar background is given as the five-elements and twelve-branch day count.
src: Gogen Yurai Jiten: Doyo no ushi
Unasei: why eel on Doyo no ushi

name: Kagawa anmochi-zoni
text: Kagawa's New Year zoni: round mochi filled with sweet bean paste, simmered in a white-miso soup made with iriko (dried sardine) dashi.
flavor: Sweet bean paste against savory white miso.
use: New Year dish, served at home.
craft: The key detail is the iriko dashi base and the bean-filled round mochi. The results seen do not give miso ratio or mochi-cooking method.

name: Nara kinako-zoni
text: A Nara zoni in white-miso broth with round mochi and other ingredients, where the mochi is dipped in kinako (roasted soybean flour) before eating.
flavor: Savory white miso with the nutty sweetness of kinako on the mochi.
use: New Year dish, served at home.
craft: The unusual step is dipping mochi in kinako at the table. The results seen do not give broth or topping specifics.

name: Kyoto white-miso zoni
text: Kyoto's zoni is built on kombu dashi with white miso, using round mochi boiled until soft. Zoni itself is said to originate in Kyoto and Kansai and to have been white-miso based; the clear-soup (sumashi) style spread later, one source attributing this to samurai society disliking miso.
flavor: Mild, sweet white miso in a kombu base.
use: New Year dish.
craft: Round mochi is simmered soft rather than grilled. Explanations of why clear soup spread in the east come from consumer-survey and lifestyle sites, so state them as accounts, not facts.

name: Hachinohe B-1 Grand Prix
text: A contest of local cuisines for regional revitalization. The first was held in February 2006 in Hachinohe, Aomori, planned by the Hachinohe Senbei-jiru Kenkyujo, at the Hasshoku Center. It began as a souvenir project tied to the Tohoku Shinkansen extension and shifted to promoting senbei-jiru itself. Voting is by chopsticks, with rank decided by weight. It is now run by the Aibleague.
flavor: Not applicable; this is an event.
use: Venue for regional dishes to gain recognition; organizers say the B stands for brand.
craft: The common reading of B as B-grade is disputed by the organizers, who say it means brand. Use their wording when citing.
src: B-1 Grand Prix: B-grade cuisine and B-1
Senbei-jiru: birthplace of B-1 Grand Prix

name: Kyo-ryori (Kyoto cuisine)
text: Often described as an umbrella term for the five systems of Japanese cooking, including shojin ryori and honzen ryori, with emphasis on dashi and drawing out the ingredient's own umami. Chorishi education material contrasts it with honzen ryori, a samurai banquet style emphasizing appearance and volume, calling kaiseki its opposite.
flavor: Dashi-centered, restrained.
use: Reference point for kaiseki and temple cuisine in Kyoto.
craft: The definitions come from tourism, cooking-school and municipal pages and vary. The five-system claim is a description given by several sites rather than a formal standard.

name: Shojin ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine)
text: Meat-free cooking built on vegetables and legumes. It is said that the methods developed in China came to Japan with Zen monks and spread in the Kamakura period; today Kyoto temples keep the tradition.
flavor: Plant-based, with no fish or meat.
use: Served at temples and in restaurants; can anchor a vegetarian course.
craft: Dashi must be plant-based. The sources seen do not give details on how dashi is made for shojin. Check specific temples for their own rules.
src: Shoyu history: types of Japanese cuisine

name: Honzen ryori (formal tray cuisine)
text: The formal banquet style developed by the warrior class in the Muromachi period, serving several trays at once. Wikipedia describes a progression of shikisankon, sankon, kyozen and a drinking banquet, and names the Okusa, Shinji and Shijo schools. It is commonly presented around a one-soup-three-dishes core.
flavor: Used as a term for formal samurai-era banquet service.
use: Historical reference when discussing kaiseki's contrast, or ceremonial meals.
craft: The sources seen do not specify the tray count of each course or school differences; verify those from a dedicated source.
src: Shoyu history: types of Japanese cuisine

name: Osechi ryori
text: The New Year dishes packed in stacked boxes (jubako); each ingredient carries a wish expressed through wordplay or appearance. Lifestyle and cooking-site explanations (Kikkoman, Kurashiru and others) agree on the main readings, with details varying by site.
flavor: New Year dish set; individual items carry meanings.
use: Eaten during New Year.
craft: Meanings are folk interpretations from commercial and lifestyle sources, so present them as customary readings. The results seen do not give an official standard.
src: Kurashiru: meaning and origin of osechi

name: Kuromame (osechi black soybeans)
text: Black beans in the osechi, tied to the word mame (diligent, healthy), so they express a wish for health and hard work. Some explanations add that black is a color that repels evil.
flavor: Pun on mame (diligence, health).
use: One of the osechi iwai-zakana.
craft: Meaning only; the results seen give no cooking method.
src: Kurashiru: meaning and origin of osechi

name: Kazunoko (herring roe)
text: Herring roe in the osechi; the large number of eggs stands for abundant descendants. A pun on nishin (herring) is also read as a wish for the parents' health and longevity.
flavor: Wish for many descendants.
use: Osechi ingredient.
craft: Meaning only; no preparation details appear in the sources seen.
src: Kurashiru: meaning and origin of osechi

name: Tazukuri / gomame (osechi dried sardines)
text: Small sardines in the osechi. The name is explained by the use of sardines as fertilizer in rice fields, so the dish prays for a good harvest. It is also written 'gomame' (five-ten-thousand rice).
flavor: Wish for a good harvest.
use: Osechi ingredient.
craft: The fertilizer origin is repeated by several sites, but details vary. The results seen give no preparation details.
src: Kurashiru: meaning and origin of osechi

name: Datemaki (osechi rolled omelet)
text: A rolled sweet omelet in the osechi. The roll resembles a scroll, associated with study and culture, and the name is said to come from date (showy, stylish).
flavor: Wish for learning and culture.
use: Osechi ingredient.
craft: Explanations of the name vary by site; the results seen give no recipe.

name: Kurikinton (osechi chestnut paste)
text: Chestnut and sweet potato dish in the osechi. Its golden color is likened to treasure, wishing for wealth. Chestnut is also a lucky food as 'kachiguri' (victory chestnut).
flavor: Wish for wealth and success.
use: Osechi ingredient.
craft: The results seen cover meaning only; no preparation details.
src: Kurashiru: meaning and origin of osechi

name: Konbumaki (osechi kelp roll)
text: Kelp rolls in the osechi. Konbu sounds like yorokobu (to rejoice), so they stand for joy, and they are tied to wishes for long life and many descendants.
flavor: Pun on yorokobu (rejoice).
use: Osechi ingredient.
craft: Meaning only; the results seen do not give the filling or simmering method.

name: Kohaku namasu (red-white daikon salad)
text: Daikon and carrot salad in the osechi. The red and white echo celebratory mizuhiki cords, expressing a wish for peace.
flavor: Wish for peace and calm.
use: Osechi ingredient.
craft: Meaning only; no cutting or seasoning details appear in the sources seen.

name: Sakizuke (first kaiseki dish)
text: The opening dish of a kaiseki or kaiseki-style course, equivalent to an otoshi or appetizer.
flavor: Course opener.
use: First plate of a banquet-style course.
craft: Position can vary by restaurant. The sources note courses differ, and banquet kaiseki has no strict rules on count or order.

name: Mukozuke (raw dish placed at the front)
text: A dish of sashimi or namasu placed at the front of the tray in kaiseki.
flavor: Raw course.
use: Sashimi or vinegared course; in tea kaiseki it sits with rice and soup.
craft: In tea kaiseki the base is rice, soup and mukozuke, followed by simmered bowl, grilled dish, small clear soup, hassun, then yuto and pickles.

name: Wanmono (soup course)
text: A clear-soup-style bowl course. In tea kaiseki the equivalent is the nimono-wan, a simmered dish served in a bowl.
flavor: Soup bowl course.
use: Follows the opener in a banquet course.
craft: Tea kaiseki and banquet kaiseki place it differently; confirm the order for the style in question.

name: Hassun (sea-and-mountain tray)
text: A tray, about 24 cm on each side, on which seasonal sea and mountain delicacies are arranged as an accompaniment to sake.
flavor: Sake-snack course.
use: In tea kaiseki it follows the small clear soup.
craft: Position varies by restaurant and source; some sources put it near the start.
src: JFCF Musubi Plus: hassun at home

name: Shiizakana (extra dish for the sake)
text: A richly seasoned simmered, dressed or fried dish served to keep the drinking going in banquet-style courses.
flavor: Stronger-flavored dish.
use: Placed after the grilled dish in a banquet course.
craft: Not fixed in the order; check how the house sequences it.

name: Tomewan (closing soup)
text: The soup that ends the meal, often miso soup, served with rice and pickles in a banquet course.
flavor: Closing soup.
use: Final savory course before dessert.
craft: Comes with rice and pickles in the sequence given by several sources.

name: Mizugashi (fruit dessert course)
text: The dessert that ends a banquet-style meal, usually fruit or sherbet. In tea kaiseki, a main sweet and thick tea close the meal.
flavor: Final sweet course.
use: Last course.
craft: Banquet order: sakizuke, wanmono, mukozuke, grilled, shiizakana, rice-soup-pickles, mizugashi.
